title: Talking Export Control Alignment, New 232s, and Trump's Budget Request with Kate Koren
transcriptText:
[music]
>> I'm Scott. I'm Bill. And we're the Trade
Guys.
You're listening to the Trade Guys, a
podcast produced by CSIS, [music]
where we talk about trade in terms that
everyone can understand. I'm Alex
Kissling, [music] and I'm here with
Scott Miller and Bill Reinsch, the CSIS
Trade Guys.
Thanks for listening to the Trade Guys.
This is Trade Guy Scott. On this week's
episode, we're joined by Kate Cullen,
Deputy Director of the CSIS Economics
Program and the Scholl Chair in
International Business. Kate's a veteran
of the Commerce Department's Bureau of
Industry and Security, and we're going
to talk with her about all things export
controls. Join us for this and more on
today's episode of the Trade Guys.
[music]
Well, welcome everybody back to another
episode of Trade Guys. It's Trade Guy
Bill here along with Scott. And a
special guest today, we have Kate Cullen
with us. Kate is the new Deputy Director
of the Economics Program and Scholl
Chair in International Business at CSIS.
She arrived in January after 3 years at
the Department of Commerce Bureau of
Industry and Security. She was the
Acting Director for the Office of
Technology Evaluation, which meant she
led research and analysis on to inform
policy development and monitor
effectiveness of our export controls.
She has an educational background in
computer science and computer
engineering, and worked in the
intelligence community before joining
the IS. She is with us because one of
the topics today is, you might figure
out from her bio,
export controls, which we haven't talked
about in a while.
And uh there's a lot going on in that
field, and we'll probably be talking
about it again from time to time as the
administration takes new actions. And I
want to begin uh with talking with Kate
about actually two pieces of legislation
that have been introduced, one recently
and one a little less recently. The big
thing in Congress, as everybody knows,
coming up with acronyms that that are
pronounceable.
So, we have the MATCH Act, M A T C H,
and the STRIDE Act, both of which are
designed to deal with how we can better
get allied coordination on export
controls. So, Kate, maybe you can start
us off by talking about the legislation
and your views on it. Thank you both,
Bill and Scott, for having me on. It's a
pleasure to be here. As you mentioned,
there's multiple uh export control
legislation sort of kicking around
Congress. Just saw an article in the
Washington Post that says the House
Foreign Affairs Committee uh is planning
to mark up both the MATCH Act and the
STRIDE Act on April 22nd, along with
maybe up to eight other pieces of export
control legislation. So, a lot
happening.
I'm going to start with the MATCH Act,
which is the newer and the more
interesting in some ways of the two
bills. It's certainly the more
stringent. So, what the MATCH Act is
fundamentally trying to do, it's trying
to solve two overarching problems. The
first being the unlevel playing field
for US and allied companies on
semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
This has been an issue since the first
wave of semiconductor controls in 2022,
because US firms are fully blocked from
selling to any of the listed Chinese
fabs. So, they can't sell any type of
equipment, they can't sell them a
pencil. But, allied firms can sell
older, less sensitive equipment to
those.
So, that's a an area that's an
unintentional misalignment that causes
the policy to, you know, not function as
intended. Because instead of, you know,
the entity-listed firms that the US
government believes are directly
contributing to China's military
modernization, instead of those firms
not getting the equipment, they just get
them from a non-US firm.
The other unlevel playing field issue
that the MATCH Act seeks to resolve is
on servicing. US firms can't provide
servicing to existing equipment inside
entity-listed fabs, but allied firms,
mainly Netherlands and Japan, can and
do. So, why is servicing an important
part of this?
So, servicing is a huge interest to
really all of the firms across the
board. It's a lot of money. In their
estimates, it's up to about a billion
dollars worth of current income for
ASML, the Netherlands company that makes
lithography equipment. For US firms, it
basically meant they were essentially
forced to abandon their equipment in
those fabs, as they could no longer
service them, they could no longer
upkeep them. So, there's certainly a
large business interest in it. On the US
side, the security aspect of it is if
the assessment is that these particular
fabs, these facilities, are producing
chips, they're producing items that are
directly supporting, you know, the
People's Liberation Army, and things
that the US government does not want to
be supported,
that by allowing the existing equipment
there to be maintained
is in further support of that and, you
know, should not be allowed. In
practice, there's definitely uh been
indications that as a way of getting
around it, cuz the way this is enacted
is through US persons restriction, that
Chinese uh repair services recruit from
the trained US service providers, and
then, you know, recruit them, have them
become Chinese citizens, and continue to
do servicing.
The reason I I asked the question was
because, you know, these these are
large, very, very complicated, and very
delicate machines that need constant
TLC. And uh if they don't get them, they
stop functioning.
And so, when companies, whether they're
in China or anywhere, buy them, they
usually come along with a maintenance
and service package, sometimes for the
most sophisticated machines with a team
that is actually co-located at the
destination. It just moves with the
machine, and their job job is to make
sure it keeps running. So, controlling
services is an important element of any
kind of a control program, because if
you don't permit the services to be
provided, basically the machines
eventually will, sooner or later, and in
some cases sooner, will break down. So,
it's an important tool that the United
States has, which hasn't always been
exercised very much, but uh this bill, I
guess, would address that. Talk to us a
little bit about obtaining multilateral
cooperation. How hard or easy is that,
and is this bill going about it the
right way? Yes, you make an excellent
point on the servicing controls, and you
know, the effort the US is controlling
uh you know, the servicing to those
entity-listed fabs, and has been, you
know, trying very hard for a while to
get that cooperation for allied firms to
do the same. Uh cuz exactly like you
said, very sophisticated equipment that
without that servicing will eventually
break down. The way that the MATCH Act
tries to solve these problems is the US
government uh has been trying basically
since the first wave of controls came
out in 2022 to get uh alignment on both
of these issues and others. But, it is
very difficult. There are different
legislative frameworks and authorities
in different countries that make some
things, you know, much easier or, you
know, some cases nearly impossible to
enact than others. And there's also a
large business interest. Something like
33% of ASML's sales uh in 2025 were to
China. It has proven very tricky to get
this alignment. There's been ongoing
diplomatic negotiations really, I think,
since this kicked off. There has been a
lot of very quiet, but very substantial
alignment that was achieved, but these
gaps remain. So, the way the MATCH Act
seeks to do that, it is very
prescriptive. It directs State and
Commerce to first try and get allies.
Doesn't name Netherlands and Japan, but
that's primarily what it's talking
about, to adopt these new controls.
Those are really the only two, aren't
they? The Netherlands and Japan? Or are
there others?
>> There are others. They're just much less
down So, for DUV, it's only them, but
for other subcomponents, there are
others.
So, it seeks to get them to adopt these
matching controls and new controls. That
was the second problem that Bill's
trying to solve. Tries to get these
countries to also control DUV equipment,
which they make, primarily made by
Netherlands. Now, for our listeners in
real lingo, DUV is deep ultraviolet
immersion lithography, right? And that's
that's highly specialized technology,
and it's what the Dutch firm ASML does
better than anyone else. Yes, thank you,
Scott. Yes. So, EUV, uh extreme
ultraviolet light lithography, uh is the
uh most advanced version of that
equipment that only ASML makes, and that
is currently controlled. That was part
of the the initial uh negotiations.
Initially, the US asserted
extraterritorial authority in 2022 over
it, and eventually then the Netherlands
agreed to enact the soft controls, and
now controls that.
But, DUV is sort of one step down, but
still highly sophisticated. It's made
primarily by ASML, but also by some
Japanese firms,
and not by any US firms. But, the US
strongly you wants that DUV technology
equipment to be controlled as well, on
the basis that China could use this as a
workaround for the controls on DUV
equipment, through some sophisticated
engineering techniques, and also just by
mass amounts of production. Seems to me
that the important thing, or maybe the
controversial thing, if that's the right
word, that the MATCH Act does, is it
wants to assert extraterritorial control
over DUV equipment, the deep ultraviolet
equipment, even though we have not
always previously controlled all of
that, and in fact ASML for years has had
substantial sales of precisely that
equipment to China and other customers.
So, in other words, we're clawing back
and expanding controls on things that
previously had been permitted to be
sold. Two questions. Is that a good
idea? And is that even viable? Yeah,
those are both very good questions.
You're exactly right. It is seeking to
both matching those EUV-based controls
and the servicing controls, but then
also expanding the controls to
lower-level technology. EUV is a is a
step down.
Whether that's advisable, there is a
valid rationale in terms of, you know,
what China can do with the equipment. I
don't want to, you know, undermine that
argument cuz it is a real argument.
There's things like multi-patterning
techniques and other, you know, kind of
known ways to use the equipment to to
ends that, you know, we have an interest
in preventing. On the other hand, they
already have a lot of it. There's been a
lot of sales. There's been a lot of
sales, especially since 2022, you know,
of EUV equipment. They have, whether
that's stockpiling or whether that's for
actual capacity, is hard to tell. But,
they have a whole heck of a lot of it
already, and they are able to make their
own. They have demonstrated the machines
exist. They're in production. They're
not as good as the ASML machines, and
they are not able to make enough of them
now, but it's a question of, you know,
time really of, you know, how long it
will take to get there. And how,
basically, how, you know, how much are
you getting for this? And because of the
way that, you know, this bill recommends
going about getting it, you're paying a
fairly high cost in the sense of what
you're sort of risking in terms of the
partnership, the multilateral
agreements, but also the risk of strong
retaliation from China.
You know, if this were to, you know, go
into effect, if this were to happen,
it's pretty much a guarantee that you
would get an extreme reaction from
China, and it would go not just against
the US, but they would take, presumably,
strong action against the Netherlands
for doing this, which would then even
further strain the relationship. And
something that concerns me is
you know, designing out US technology
from, you know, ASML EUV equipment to
the extent where the US couldn't assert
jurisdiction would be extremely complex
and expensive, like incredibly
difficult. But, where is that tipping
point? Since you're an insider, Kate,
let me ask you a couple or former
insider, there's a couple of questions
come to mind cuz I looked at the
legislation as it is in draft form. And
it's a typical early congressional
product. It has great name and a
wonderful press release and a somewhat
disappointing draft bill that is
referred to at least the most of the
current bill is not even a has doesn't
have a bill number. It has it's called a
discussion draft, and it's about 16
pages long. So,
given the formative stages that we seem
to be at and your knowledge of how these
negotiations might proceed, what do you
think that the administration actually
needs in terms of statutory authority?
And what kinds of changes would you
advise that would make it more effective
in the result that everyone seems to
want? It's a great question.
So, what would be the quick timeline on
this with, you know,
reportedly this going to be, you know,
marked up on the 22nd. I expect that the
intent is to get this into the NDAA, you
know, the defense authorization bill,
which is, you know, a must-pass bill as
a way to get it through. And so, there
will be, you know, changes presumably in
that markup. It'll be interesting to see
if, you know, GOP leadership pushes back
on this as they have with the AI
Overwatch Act and other chip legislation
that somewhat goes in a different
direction than the approach the
president has taken on chip sales and
chip exports.
My approach to this would be
to, as opposed to going in with the
stated threat, basically, that what
that, you know, we're going into a
negotiation, but if you don't agree to
our terms, we are going to take
authority and assert authority, and
you know, if you won't control it, we
will control it for you.
I think there's a different approach you
could take to get what you really need
in terms of the alignment on the
existing controls as they are. You can
use the sort of this,
that you now have, you know, publicly
put out in a in a draft form, threat
about EUV equipment as a, you know, we
will drop that if you will meet us here.
There's the stronger national security
argument, to my mind, on the sales and
servicing to the end users of fabs than
there is on extending the controls
further to older equipment. So, that
would be how I would approach it. Well,
great. Sounds like a fine mess that the
yeah, controls people have got
themselves in. Fortunately, you have
broad underlying authorities, and you
have some multilateral fora in which to
discuss this. Are any of the existing
discussion forums useful in this regard,
or they all they all have actors like
Russia or people that we don't want at
the table involved in the discussion?
Well,
you know, this is an interesting
approach to export controls in that the
draft bill reads a lot almost like a
draft regulation, which is a little
unusual. So, it's very prescriptive in
what the regulation should be, which is
not the typical order of things.
Generally, you know, we would see
something like this, the idea these
things coming, you know, from the
Commerce Department directly and not
coming through legislation directing the
Commerce Department to do so. Well, this
sounds like we've got a lot of things to
watch, and we thank you for giving us
the really knowledgeable expert
view of what
seems incredibly complicated to anybody
who's a casual observer of export
controls. Very much. Bill, you've been
in this business for a long time. You
think this will work?
I'm skeptical. Basically, putting under
control things that have been released
in the past is always a difficult
exercise. The economic stake is
significant. ASML, in particular, has
made a lot of money selling these
things. The United States government in
the past has let them sell these things.
So, to kind of take a step backwards now
is going to be difficult diplomatically.
It was hard enough, you know, in the
beginning, as Kate will knows in 2022,
to get the degree of cooperation that
the Biden administration was able to
get. The Trump administration, as we've
talked about in other contexts, tends to
be more stick-oriented than
carrot-oriented, and will be inclined, I
think, to use its extra-territorial
reach the and the foreign direct product
rule to try to cut these things off if
the Dutch and the Japanese don't
cooperate. And that will then produce, I
think, the two things that Kate was
talking about, which is retaliation from
China and also acceleration of their own
efforts to develop their own technology
that excludes anything that is US-based.
Maybe I can ask one last question on
this for Kate.
We do seem to be in an odd position
where, despite the acrimony, the Chinese
and the United States are actually in
some respects pursuing similar policies.
We are trying to prevent them from
getting our stuff, and they are trying
to pressure their companies not to use
our stuff and to develop their own. So,
in an odd way, aren't our policies kind
of aligned? When you pose it that way, I
aligned is not exactly how I would have
phrased it, but they are converging.
Yeah, I think the flaw in that argument
is that, and you noted that, is that
they're not producing now at the scale
that they need to meet their own
domestic needs, and they'll need to
continue to rely on Western sources, at
least in the in the short run. What
could they do in retaliation that would
be serious? So, you know, we've reached
sort of a place of, you know, detente,
and we'll see, you know, what happens at
the next, you know, Trump and Xi summit
on this in May. But, their ability to
cut off your access to critical minerals
very real and has a, you know, very
large impact. There's no reason to think
they wouldn't do the same with Japan,
and there's no reason to think they
wouldn't do the same with Netherlands.
And, you know, they've built the
infrastructure to do this, and while
there's a lot of, you know, really good
and solid efforts going on to, you know,
develop alternate, you know, supply
chains, you know, for these minerals,
it's going to take time. As long as
we're in that place, you know, we are
very vulnerable to this retaliation. And
they've shown themselves, you know, very
capable and willing and ready to, you
know, adapt and really meet us, you
know, tit for tat.
Well, for those of you who followed the
Supreme Court arguments and thought we
were done with tariffs for a while,
we're sorry to disappoint you, but there
are more tariff announcements from
elsewhere in the Commerce Department
this week, including Section 232
national security tariffs on metals,
that is, steel, aluminum, and copper,
and pharmaceuticals. Now, this is one
where the more I research this, the more
confused I got, but there were already
tariffs on metals based on the the
amount of and these are products made
with with steel, aluminum, and copper,
as well as steel, aluminum, and copper.
As if this weren't complicated enough,
there is now a a plan to take an entire
product where steel, aluminum, or copper
makes up more than 15% by weight and
charge a flat 25% tariff on the entire
value of the product, which seems like
it covers a lot and may make things even
more complicated. So, on the steel side,
we're fortunate to have Bill on the
podcast because of his long years with
the steel caucus as a congressional
staffer to the steel caucus in Congress
and the deep knowledge of all the myriad
twists and turns of the steel business.
Are we really protecting anything, Bill,
or are we just making life difficult for
users of things, not just steel, but
users of products that happen to be
constructed with steel, copper, or
aluminum?
Well, the ostensible goal of this change
is to make things simpler. It probably
does make things simpler, but doesn't
necessarily make them better for for
anybody, really. Simple is because of
the most famous example that came up has
been the dental floss example.
Because the previous dental floss
>> Yes. Yes, the previous rule was that if
you were importing a product that
contains steel,
you had to pay the 50% tariff on that
portion of the product that was steel.
And that turned out to be
extraordinarily complex because most
people don't think about how much steel
is in their product. And sometimes it's
de minimis. Dental floss being the case.
For those of you that floss, know that
floss is not a steel product. On each
little container of floss, there's this
tiny little steel thing at the top that
you use to cut the floss. Under the
previous system, they would have had to
pay a 50% tariff on the value of that
piece, irrespective of the value of the
rest of the item. That was a calculation
nightmare trying to figure out and
multiply that by many different cases.
This was designed to simplify that
because it just says, "If your metal
content is under 15%,
which it would be in the case of dental
floss, there's no steel tariff, period.
You just pay what that country is
paying. If it's more than 15%, then the
new thing is, instead of paying a
percentage based on the value of the
steel content, you're just going to pay
a flat 25%. Depending on the product and
depending on the amount of steel
content, that may or may not be an
increase in what you had been paying."
It would be a simplification. So, I
guess, you know, if you're concerned
about paperwork, that you know, that
gets you something. What it's doing, I
think, is probably not having the
intended effect. The domestic steel
industry, I'm reasonably confident, is
happy. They're making more money.
Whether they're hiring more workers is a
different story. Steel working work
employment has been declining for for
years, largely as a product of
technology, not for other reasons, but
the industry is there. I think that the
issue that has had the biggest negative
impact on the economy has been the
downstream tariffs. Tariffs on basic
steel are not new, and there's been a
whole network of anti-dumping and
countervailing duty tariffs on steel for
40 years in various permutations,
various countries, various levels. The
new Trump wrinkle is downstream
products. So, things that contain steel
suddenly are having 50% or depending on
the country, if because if you've cut
deals like in the UK and the EU too,
it's supposed to be down to 10% in the
case of UK or 15% in the case of the EU,
but it's still substantial compared to
the past. And this is awkward because a
lot of what those things are are parts
and components that go into end
products, the most obvious one being
automobiles. Right. So, what we have
done is make making cars more expensive
to the extent that people are importing
car parts from overseas. Now, there's a
special treatment for Canadian and
Mexican car parts, so it's not a huge
thing, but the point of it is to
persuade companies to reshore and do
their manufacturing here,
>> Sure.
>> buy their steel here, and make their
steel parts and components out of
American steel. There are ironies to
this, though, if you if you if you just
noticed uh today's report was that
apparently Trump's ballroom is going to
be using foreign steel. Well, that's
nice. Which is a little bit inconsistent
with the spirit of the thing, I would
say. It's being supplied by
ArcelorMittal, which actually has been
for a long time was an American company.
They bought Bethlehem Steel, as I
recall, but over the last few years,
they've not entirely, but more or less
gotten out of the US business and are
really a global company. And I think the
ballroom steel is is going to be
imported. But no one has yet asked or
gotten out of the Trump administration
explanation of why they feel they need
to do that as opposed to buy it from US
Steel or Cleveland Cliffs or other
producers.
So, I don't think it's having the
desired reshoring effect. On the other
hand, too soon to say. Yeah, most of
these things don't don't wind up
working. Yeah, exactly.
>> Yes, that's right. And they certainly by
making things more complicated, you make
it more expensive to manufacture in the
United States. So, congratulations on
that. Your dental floss example reminded
me of the famous Lacey Act extensions.
Lacey Act prevented sort of illegally
harvested wildlife animals in birds in
particular. And there was a concern
raised about illegal logging. And so,
some excited member of Congress decided,
"Well, let's just extend the Lacey Act
to the plant kingdom as well as the
animal kingdom."
And they did, and then they figured out
that the plants are in everything like
paper. So, all of a sudden, the Lacey
there was Lacey Act compliance for cars
because of the owner's manual and the
air filter, both of which were paper
products. So, [laughter]
they stopped themselves before they
legislated again, but I guess we can
repent at leisure for some of this. It's
an axiom. You mess with the market and
there are unintended downstream
consequences every single time.
>> definitely. Can you talk about the
pharma the pharmaceutical thing for a
couple minutes just so
>> Yes. Yes, I think that's an interesting
one because well, you can understand the
concern about the need to have
production capacity on pharmaceuticals.
The United States was always a good
place to do confined chemistry. I think
with today's plentiful hydrocarbons in
the market, it's an even more attractive
place to do fine chemistry. But the drug
section 232,
it appears to me that while it's on the
surface quite punitive for foreign
manufacturers, the exceptions seem to
swallow the rule by the time you get
through with it because there's a 100%
tariff on imported drugs made by
companies that refuse to have US
production or refuse to commit to US
production.
In terms of pharmaceutical producers,
there are a number of bilateral
agreements and the so-called most
favored nation clause because the Trump
administration as well as trying to
reshore or have US production of
pharmaceuticals, they are trying to
match global pricing and reduce costs to
the consumer. So, these goals obviously
collide. And I think with the number of
exceptions of if you have a bilateral,
if you accepted the most favored nation,
if you made a plan to have capacity in
the United States, and keep in mind, it
probably takes 7 to 10 years to build a
full-scale pharmaceutical plant to FDA
compliant standards. So, it's a
commitment is a long time away from a
factory producing the product. Having
said all that, it's a very high tariff
on probably no one by the time we get
done with it, but
I don't know. Do you have another view,
Bill? I don't think the exceptions in
100% swallow the rule, but it's a it's
an illustration of what Trump has been
trying to do in [snorts] a lot of areas,
which is reshoring.
>> Yes. And in the pharma case, it's
explicit. You know, if you commit to
building the factory here, you get a
deal.
And a lot of companies are doing that.
And
as Scott said, it's probably going to
take a while to bring that to fruition,
but the unknown, I think, at this point
is is that going to raise or lower drug
prices? I mean, this is also part of a
campaign. A big priority for for
actually both parties has been to lower
the price of drugs. The American public
thinks drug prices are too high. If you
look at the data, drug prices here are
really are higher than in many other
countries. There are reasons for that,
one being other countries have national
health programs that that subsidize
them, but we do have high drug prices.
It's clearly a politically sensitive
issue. Both parties are competing to say
that they are the better ones most
likely to reduce drug prices.
And now we have a policy that is
designed to force companies to produce
here,
which will almost certainly be more
expensive. It's very likely. And you can
make the argument then you you switch to
the security argument. You know, we need
to have our own production capabilities
of this stuff. We don't want to rely on
the Chinese for medicine.
I mean, I get that. That's legitimate.
But what we've got, as we've seen in
other cases, is multiple conflicting
goals.
>> Yes. If you don't want to rely on the
Chinese and you want to have low prices,
it's hard to achieve both of those
things at the same time.
>> Yes, but fortunately, we're talking
about Washington, where talking out of
both sides of your mouth is a basic
employment skill. So,
we have plenty of practitioners.
>> I used to do that a lot. I know it well.
>> Yes, we're all we're sort of recovering
in that category, at least Bill and I
are. Since we have Kate with us, a
recent veteran of the Commerce
Department, we decided to close with a
Commerce Department story, and that's
about the president's budget for various
Commerce functions in the coming year.
It's interesting only because there's an
overall 10% reduction in non-defense
discretionary spending implied in the
president's budget. And that slices a
number of different ways in the Commerce
Department, in part because the Commerce
Department is the Department of
Miscellaneous in a lot of respects.
There are many many, many functions in
there, but also because certain
functions like information security,
which manages export controls, is a
vital defense function. So, there's
there's a lot of business that is
non-defense in the Commerce Department.
So, Kate, could you give us an overall
look at what you think the president's
trying to accomplish in the budget he
just presented?
I'd just say while she's getting ready,
Scott's comment about the Department of
Everything reminds me when I was in the
Commerce Department we went through a
two years of the Republicans trying to
eliminate it,
which is a fascinating story in and of

segments.text: [music] >> I'm Scott. I'm Bill. And we're the Trade Guys. You're listening to the Trade Guys, a podcast produced by CSIS, [music] where we talk about trade in terms that everyone can understand. I'm Alex Kissling, [music] and I'm here with

Scott Miller and Bill Reinsch, the CSIS Trade Guys. Thanks for listening to the Trade Guys. This is Trade Guy Scott. On this week's episode, we're joined by Kate Cullen, Deputy Director of the CSIS Economics Program and the Scholl Chair in

International Business. Kate's a veteran of the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, and we're going to talk with her about all things export controls. Join us for this and more on today's episode of the Trade Guys. [music]

Well, welcome everybody back to another episode of Trade Guys. It's Trade Guy Bill here along with Scott. And a special guest today, we have Kate Cullen with us. Kate is the new Deputy Director of the Economics Program and Scholl

Chair in International Business at CSIS. She arrived in January after 3 years at the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security. She was the Acting Director for the Office of Technology Evaluation, which meant she

led research and analysis on to inform policy development and monitor effectiveness of our export controls. She has an educational background in computer science and computer engineering, and worked in the intelligence community before joining

the IS. She is with us because one of the topics today is, you might figure out from her bio, export controls, which we haven't talked about in a while. And uh there's a lot going on in that field, and we'll probably be talking

about it again from time to time as the administration takes new actions. And I want to begin uh with talking with Kate about actually two pieces of legislation that have been introduced, one recently and one a little less recently. The big

thing in Congress, as everybody knows, coming up with acronyms that that are pronounceable. So, we have the MATCH Act, M A T C H, and the STRIDE Act, both of which are designed to deal with how we can better get allied coordination on export

controls. So, Kate, maybe you can start us off by talking about the legislation and your views on it. Thank you both, Bill and Scott, for having me on. It's a pleasure to be here. As you mentioned, there's multiple uh export control

legislation sort of kicking around Congress. Just saw an article in the Washington Post that says the House Foreign Affairs Committee uh is planning to mark up both the MATCH Act and the STRIDE Act on April 22nd, along with

maybe up to eight other pieces of export control legislation. So, a lot happening. I'm going to start with the MATCH Act, which is the newer and the more interesting in some ways of the two bills. It's certainly the more stringent. So, what the MATCH Act is

fundamentally trying to do, it's trying to solve two overarching problems. The first being the unlevel playing field for US and allied companies on semiconductor manufacturing equipment. This has been an issue since the first

wave of semiconductor controls in 2022, because US firms are fully blocked from selling to any of the listed Chinese fabs. So, they can't sell any type of equipment, they can't sell them a pencil. But, allied firms can sell older, less sensitive equipment to

those. So, that's a an area that's an unintentional misalignment that causes the policy to, you know, not function as intended. Because instead of, you know, the entity-listed firms that the US government believes are directly contributing to China's military

modernization, instead of those firms not getting the equipment, they just get them from a non-US firm. The other unlevel playing field issue that the MATCH Act seeks to resolve is on servicing. US firms can't provide servicing to existing equipment inside

entity-listed fabs, but allied firms, mainly Netherlands and Japan, can and do. So, why is servicing an important part of this? So, servicing is a huge interest to really all of the firms across the board. It's a lot of money. In their

estimates, it's up to about a billion dollars worth of current income for ASML, the Netherlands company that makes lithography equipment. For US firms, it basically meant they were essentially forced to abandon their equipment in

those fabs, as they could no longer service them, they could no longer upkeep them. So, there's certainly a large business interest in it. On the US side, the security aspect of it is if the assessment is that these particular

fabs, these facilities, are producing chips, they're producing items that are directly supporting, you know, the People's Liberation Army, and things that the US government does not want to be supported, that by allowing the existing equipment

there to be maintained is in further support of that and, you know, should not be allowed. In practice, there's definitely uh been indications that as a way of getting around it, cuz the way this is enacted is through US persons restriction, that

Chinese uh repair services recruit from the trained US service providers, and then, you know, recruit them, have them become Chinese citizens, and continue to do servicing. The reason I I asked the question was because, you know, these these are

large, very, very complicated, and very delicate machines that need constant TLC. And uh if they don't get them, they stop functioning. And so, when companies, whether they're in China or anywhere, buy them, they usually come along with a maintenance

and service package, sometimes for the most sophisticated machines with a team that is actually co-located at the destination. It just moves with the machine, and their job job is to make sure it keeps running. So, controlling

services is an important element of any kind of a control program, because if you don't permit the services to be provided, basically the machines eventually will, sooner or later, and in some cases sooner, will break down. So,

it's an important tool that the United States has, which hasn't always been exercised very much, but uh this bill, I guess, would address that. Talk to us a little bit about obtaining multilateral cooperation. How hard or easy is that,

and is this bill going about it the right way? Yes, you make an excellent point on the servicing controls, and you know, the effort the US is controlling uh you know, the servicing to those entity-listed fabs, and has been, you

know, trying very hard for a while to get that cooperation for allied firms to do the same. Uh cuz exactly like you said, very sophisticated equipment that without that servicing will eventually break down. The way that the MATCH Act

tries to solve these problems is the US government uh has been trying basically since the first wave of controls came out in 2022 to get uh alignment on both of these issues and others. But, it is very difficult. There are different

legislative frameworks and authorities in different countries that make some things, you know, much easier or, you know, some cases nearly impossible to enact than others. And there's also a large business interest. Something like

33% of ASML's sales uh in 2025 were to China. It has proven very tricky to get this alignment. There's been ongoing diplomatic negotiations really, I think, since this kicked off. There has been a lot of very quiet, but very substantial

alignment that was achieved, but these gaps remain. So, the way the MATCH Act seeks to do that, it is very prescriptive. It directs State and Commerce to first try and get allies. Doesn't name Netherlands and Japan, but that's primarily what it's talking

about, to adopt these new controls. Those are really the only two, aren't they? The Netherlands and Japan? Or are there others? >> There are others. They're just much less down So, for DUV, it's only them, but for other subcomponents, there are others.

So, it seeks to get them to adopt these matching controls and new controls. That was the second problem that Bill's trying to solve. Tries to get these countries to also control DUV equipment, which they make, primarily made by

Netherlands. Now, for our listeners in real lingo, DUV is deep ultraviolet immersion lithography, right? And that's that's highly specialized technology, and it's what the Dutch firm ASML does better than anyone else. Yes, thank you,

Scott. Yes. So, EUV, uh extreme ultraviolet light lithography, uh is the uh most advanced version of that equipment that only ASML makes, and that is currently controlled. That was part of the the initial uh negotiations. Initially, the US asserted

extraterritorial authority in 2022 over it, and eventually then the Netherlands agreed to enact the soft controls, and now controls that. But, DUV is sort of one step down, but still highly sophisticated. It's made primarily by ASML, but also by some

Japanese firms, and not by any US firms. But, the US strongly you wants that DUV technology equipment to be controlled as well, on the basis that China could use this as a workaround for the controls on DUV equipment, through some sophisticated

engineering techniques, and also just by mass amounts of production. Seems to me that the important thing, or maybe the controversial thing, if that's the right word, that the MATCH Act does, is it wants to assert extraterritorial control

over DUV equipment, the deep ultraviolet equipment, even though we have not always previously controlled all of that, and in fact ASML for years has had substantial sales of precisely that equipment to China and other customers.

So, in other words, we're clawing back and expanding controls on things that previously had been permitted to be sold. Two questions. Is that a good idea? And is that even viable? Yeah, those are both very good questions. You're exactly right. It is seeking to

both matching those EUV-based controls and the servicing controls, but then also expanding the controls to lower-level technology. EUV is a is a step down. Whether that's advisable, there is a valid rationale in terms of, you know,

what China can do with the equipment. I don't want to, you know, undermine that argument cuz it is a real argument. There's things like multi-patterning techniques and other, you know, kind of known ways to use the equipment to to

ends that, you know, we have an interest in preventing. On the other hand, they already have a lot of it. There's been a lot of sales. There's been a lot of sales, especially since 2022, you know, of EUV equipment. They have, whether

that's stockpiling or whether that's for actual capacity, is hard to tell. But, they have a whole heck of a lot of it already, and they are able to make their own. They have demonstrated the machines exist. They're in production. They're

not as good as the ASML machines, and they are not able to make enough of them now, but it's a question of, you know, time really of, you know, how long it will take to get there. And how, basically, how, you know, how much are

you getting for this? And because of the way that, you know, this bill recommends going about getting it, you're paying a fairly high cost in the sense of what you're sort of risking in terms of the partnership, the multilateral

agreements, but also the risk of strong retaliation from China. You know, if this were to, you know, go into effect, if this were to happen, it's pretty much a guarantee that you would get an extreme reaction from China, and it would go not just against

the US, but they would take, presumably, strong action against the Netherlands for doing this, which would then even further strain the relationship. And something that concerns me is you know, designing out US technology from, you know, ASML EUV equipment to

the extent where the US couldn't assert jurisdiction would be extremely complex and expensive, like incredibly difficult. But, where is that tipping point? Since you're an insider, Kate, let me ask you a couple or former insider, there's a couple of questions

come to mind cuz I looked at the legislation as it is in draft form. And it's a typical early congressional product. It has great name and a wonderful press release and a somewhat disappointing draft bill that is referred to at least the most of the

current bill is not even a has doesn't have a bill number. It has it's called a discussion draft, and it's about 16 pages long. So, given the formative stages that we seem to be at and your knowledge of how these negotiations might proceed, what do you

think that the administration actually needs in terms of statutory authority? And what kinds of changes would you advise that would make it more effective in the result that everyone seems to want? It's a great question. So, what would be the quick timeline on

this with, you know, reportedly this going to be, you know, marked up on the 22nd. I expect that the intent is to get this into the NDAA, you know, the defense authorization bill, which is, you know, a must-pass bill as a way to get it through. And so, there

will be, you know, changes presumably in that markup. It'll be interesting to see if, you know, GOP leadership pushes back on this as they have with the AI Overwatch Act and other chip legislation that somewhat goes in a different

direction than the approach the president has taken on chip sales and chip exports. My approach to this would be to, as opposed to going in with the stated threat, basically, that what that, you know, we're going into a negotiation, but if you don't agree to

our terms, we are going to take authority and assert authority, and you know, if you won't control it, we will control it for you. I think there's a different approach you could take to get what you really need in terms of the alignment on the

existing controls as they are. You can use the sort of this, that you now have, you know, publicly put out in a in a draft form, threat about EUV equipment as a, you know, we will drop that if you will meet us here. There's the stronger national security

argument, to my mind, on the sales and servicing to the end users of fabs than there is on extending the controls further to older equipment. So, that would be how I would approach it. Well, great. Sounds like a fine mess that the

yeah, controls people have got themselves in. Fortunately, you have broad underlying authorities, and you have some multilateral fora in which to discuss this. Are any of the existing discussion forums useful in this regard,

or they all they all have actors like Russia or people that we don't want at the table involved in the discussion? Well, you know, this is an interesting approach to export controls in that the draft bill reads a lot almost like a

draft regulation, which is a little unusual. So, it's very prescriptive in what the regulation should be, which is not the typical order of things. Generally, you know, we would see something like this, the idea these things coming, you know, from the

Commerce Department directly and not coming through legislation directing the Commerce Department to do so. Well, this sounds like we've got a lot of things to watch, and we thank you for giving us the really knowledgeable expert view of what

seems incredibly complicated to anybody who's a casual observer of export controls. Very much. Bill, you've been in this business for a long time. You think this will work? I'm skeptical. Basically, putting under control things that have been released

in the past is always a difficult exercise. The economic stake is significant. ASML, in particular, has made a lot of money selling these things. The United States government in the past has let them sell these things. So, to kind of take a step backwards now

is going to be difficult diplomatically. It was hard enough, you know, in the beginning, as Kate will knows in 2022, to get the degree of cooperation that the Biden administration was able to get. The Trump administration, as we've

talked about in other contexts, tends to be more stick-oriented than carrot-oriented, and will be inclined, I think, to use its extra-territorial reach the and the foreign direct product rule to try to cut these things off if the Dutch and the Japanese don't

cooperate. And that will then produce, I think, the two things that Kate was talking about, which is retaliation from China and also acceleration of their own efforts to develop their own technology that excludes anything that is US-based.

Maybe I can ask one last question on this for Kate. We do seem to be in an odd position where, despite the acrimony, the Chinese and the United States are actually in some respects pursuing similar policies. We are trying to prevent them from

getting our stuff, and they are trying to pressure their companies not to use our stuff and to develop their own. So, in an odd way, aren't our policies kind of aligned? When you pose it that way, I aligned is not exactly how I would have

phrased it, but they are converging. Yeah, I think the flaw in that argument is that, and you noted that, is that they're not producing now at the scale that they need to meet their own domestic needs, and they'll need to

continue to rely on Western sources, at least in the in the short run. What could they do in retaliation that would be serious? So, you know, we've reached sort of a place of, you know, detente, and we'll see, you know, what happens at

the next, you know, Trump and Xi summit on this in May. But, their ability to cut off your access to critical minerals very real and has a, you know, very large impact. There's no reason to think they wouldn't do the same with Japan,

and there's no reason to think they wouldn't do the same with Netherlands. And, you know, they've built the infrastructure to do this, and while there's a lot of, you know, really good and solid efforts going on to, you know,

develop alternate, you know, supply chains, you know, for these minerals, it's going to take time. As long as we're in that place, you know, we are very vulnerable to this retaliation. And they've shown themselves, you know, very

capable and willing and ready to, you know, adapt and really meet us, you know, tit for tat. Well, for those of you who followed the Supreme Court arguments and thought we were done with tariffs for a while, we're sorry to disappoint you, but there

are more tariff announcements from elsewhere in the Commerce Department this week, including Section 232 national security tariffs on metals, that is, steel, aluminum, and copper, and pharmaceuticals. Now, this is one where the more I research this, the more

confused I got, but there were already tariffs on metals based on the the amount of and these are products made with with steel, aluminum, and copper, as well as steel, aluminum, and copper. As if this weren't complicated enough,

there is now a a plan to take an entire product where steel, aluminum, or copper makes up more than 15% by weight and charge a flat 25% tariff on the entire value of the product, which seems like it covers a lot and may make things even

more complicated. So, on the steel side, we're fortunate to have Bill on the podcast because of his long years with the steel caucus as a congressional staffer to the steel caucus in Congress and the deep knowledge of all the myriad

twists and turns of the steel business. Are we really protecting anything, Bill, or are we just making life difficult for users of things, not just steel, but users of products that happen to be constructed with steel, copper, or aluminum?

Well, the ostensible goal of this change is to make things simpler. It probably does make things simpler, but doesn't necessarily make them better for for anybody, really. Simple is because of the most famous example that came up has

been the dental floss example. Because the previous dental floss >> Yes. Yes, the previous rule was that if you were importing a product that contains steel, you had to pay the 50% tariff on that portion of the product that was steel. And that turned out to be

extraordinarily complex because most people don't think about how much steel is in their product. And sometimes it's de minimis. Dental floss being the case. For those of you that floss, know that floss is not a steel product. On each

little container of floss, there's this tiny little steel thing at the top that you use to cut the floss. Under the previous system, they would have had to pay a 50% tariff on the value of that piece, irrespective of the value of the

rest of the item. That was a calculation nightmare trying to figure out and multiply that by many different cases. This was designed to simplify that because it just says, "If your metal content is under 15%, which it would be in the case of dental

floss, there's no steel tariff, period. You just pay what that country is paying. If it's more than 15%, then the new thing is, instead of paying a percentage based on the value of the steel content, you're just going to pay

a flat 25%. Depending on the product and depending on the amount of steel content, that may or may not be an increase in what you had been paying." It would be a simplification. So, I guess, you know, if you're concerned about paperwork, that you know, that

gets you something. What it's doing, I think, is probably not having the intended effect. The domestic steel industry, I'm reasonably confident, is happy. They're making more money. Whether they're hiring more workers is a different story. Steel working work

employment has been declining for for years, largely as a product of technology, not for other reasons, but the industry is there. I think that the issue that has had the biggest negative impact on the economy has been the downstream tariffs. Tariffs on basic

steel are not new, and there's been a whole network of anti-dumping and countervailing duty tariffs on steel for 40 years in various permutations, various countries, various levels. The new Trump wrinkle is downstream products. So, things that contain steel

suddenly are having 50% or depending on the country, if because if you've cut deals like in the UK and the EU too, it's supposed to be down to 10% in the case of UK or 15% in the case of the EU, but it's still substantial compared to

the past. And this is awkward because a lot of what those things are are parts and components that go into end products, the most obvious one being automobiles. Right. So, what we have done is make making cars more expensive

to the extent that people are importing car parts from overseas. Now, there's a special treatment for Canadian and Mexican car parts, so it's not a huge thing, but the point of it is to persuade companies to reshore and do their manufacturing here, >> Sure.

>> buy their steel here, and make their steel parts and components out of American steel. There are ironies to this, though, if you if you if you just noticed uh today's report was that apparently Trump's ballroom is going to

be using foreign steel. Well, that's nice. Which is a little bit inconsistent with the spirit of the thing, I would say. It's being supplied by ArcelorMittal, which actually has been for a long time was an American company. They bought Bethlehem Steel, as I

recall, but over the last few years, they've not entirely, but more or less gotten out of the US business and are really a global company. And I think the ballroom steel is is going to be imported. But no one has yet asked or

gotten out of the Trump administration explanation of why they feel they need to do that as opposed to buy it from US Steel or Cleveland Cliffs or other producers. So, I don't think it's having the desired reshoring effect. On the other

hand, too soon to say. Yeah, most of these things don't don't wind up working. Yeah, exactly. >> Yes, that's right. And they certainly by making things more complicated, you make it more expensive to manufacture in the United States. So, congratulations on

that. Your dental floss example reminded me of the famous Lacey Act extensions. Lacey Act prevented sort of illegally harvested wildlife animals in birds in particular. And there was a concern raised about illegal logging. And so,

some excited member of Congress decided, "Well, let's just extend the Lacey Act to the plant kingdom as well as the animal kingdom." And they did, and then they figured out that the plants are in everything like paper. So, all of a sudden, the Lacey

there was Lacey Act compliance for cars because of the owner's manual and the air filter, both of which were paper products. So, [laughter] they stopped themselves before they legislated again, but I guess we can repent at leisure for some of this. It's

an axiom. You mess with the market and there are unintended downstream consequences every single time. >> definitely. Can you talk about the pharma the pharmaceutical thing for a couple minutes just so >> Yes. Yes, I think that's an interesting

one because well, you can understand the concern about the need to have production capacity on pharmaceuticals. The United States was always a good place to do confined chemistry. I think with today's plentiful hydrocarbons in

the market, it's an even more attractive place to do fine chemistry. But the drug section 232, it appears to me that while it's on the surface quite punitive for foreign manufacturers, the exceptions seem to swallow the rule by the time you get

through with it because there's a 100% tariff on imported drugs made by companies that refuse to have US production or refuse to commit to US production. In terms of pharmaceutical producers, there are a number of bilateral agreements and the so-called most

favored nation clause because the Trump administration as well as trying to reshore or have US production of pharmaceuticals, they are trying to match global pricing and reduce costs to the consumer. So, these goals obviously

collide. And I think with the number of exceptions of if you have a bilateral, if you accepted the most favored nation, if you made a plan to have capacity in the United States, and keep in mind, it probably takes 7 to 10 years to build a

full-scale pharmaceutical plant to FDA compliant standards. So, it's a commitment is a long time away from a factory producing the product. Having said all that, it's a very high tariff on probably no one by the time we get done with it, but

I don't know. Do you have another view, Bill? I don't think the exceptions in 100% swallow the rule, but it's a it's an illustration of what Trump has been trying to do in [snorts] a lot of areas, which is reshoring. >> Yes. And in the pharma case, it's

explicit. You know, if you commit to building the factory here, you get a deal. And a lot of companies are doing that. And as Scott said, it's probably going to take a while to bring that to fruition, but the unknown, I think, at this point

is is that going to raise or lower drug prices? I mean, this is also part of a campaign. A big priority for for actually both parties has been to lower the price of drugs. The American public thinks drug prices are too high. If you

look at the data, drug prices here are really are higher than in many other countries. There are reasons for that, one being other countries have national health programs that that subsidize them, but we do have high drug prices.

It's clearly a politically sensitive issue. Both parties are competing to say that they are the better ones most likely to reduce drug prices. And now we have a policy that is designed to force companies to produce here, which will almost certainly be more

expensive. It's very likely. And you can make the argument then you you switch to the security argument. You know, we need to have our own production capabilities of this stuff. We don't want to rely on the Chinese for medicine.

I mean, I get that. That's legitimate. But what we've got, as we've seen in other cases, is multiple conflicting goals. >> Yes. If you don't want to rely on the Chinese and you want to have low prices, it's hard to achieve both of those

things at the same time. >> Yes, but fortunately, we're talking about Washington, where talking out of both sides of your mouth is a basic employment skill. So, we have plenty of practitioners. >> I used to do that a lot. I know it well.

>> Yes, we're all we're sort of recovering in that category, at least Bill and I are. Since we have Kate with us, a recent veteran of the Commerce Department, we decided to close with a Commerce Department story, and that's

about the president's budget for various Commerce functions in the coming year. It's interesting only because there's an overall 10% reduction in non-defense discretionary spending implied in the president's budget. And that slices a

number of different ways in the Commerce Department, in part because the Commerce Department is the Department of Miscellaneous in a lot of respects. There are many many, many functions in there, but also because certain functions like information security,

which manages export controls, is a vital defense function. So, there's there's a lot of business that is non-defense in the Commerce Department. So, Kate, could you give us an overall look at what you think the president's

trying to accomplish in the budget he just presented? I'd just say while she's getting ready, Scott's comment about the Department of Everything reminds me when I was in the Commerce Department we went through a two years of the Republicans trying to

eliminate it, which is a fascinating story in and of itself, but one of their prime quotes came from uh George H.W. Bush's Secretary of Commerce, Bob Mosbacher, who referred to it as the hall closet of government. Everything

you didn't know where to put, you put it at the Commerce Department. >> It wound up there somehow. And one of the things that I was tasked with doing by the secretary in the Clinton administration was trying to demonstrate

how everything is related to everything else inside the building. So, we had to figure out how the Minority Business Development Administration and the National Oceanographic Atmospheric Administration and the Bureau of of
